# Copper October 2012 - As we incorporate the news gathered during LME week and update Q3 reported production numbers, we have revised our numbers slightly for this year, but more notably, for 2013. We have been tracking mine disruptions closely and incorporating these into our production estimates as the year progressed and it is clear that output growth has once again disappointed. However, as we continue to unwind the tail end of our generic disruption against identified outages, unsurprisingly our revisions and overall balance for 2012 are not dissimilar to that presented in the last monthly publication which is for a market in broad balance. A meagre surplus of ~89kt will keep stocks at 53 days of consumption for 2012 and with three full quarters now behind us, our average price is now slightly lower at ~$7960/t ($3.61/lb). We remain of the view that cash copper quotes will trade lower over the balance of the quarter as lower anticipated Chinese cathode imports hit sentiment. - The main consensus coming out of LME week is that nobody really knows what will happen to demand next year. There are known, knowns such as European debt and known unknowns like the future Chinese leadership, while there are most certainly unknown unknowns. The one thing that everyone agreed upon was that there was little to no visibility in order books. Wood Mackenzie forecasts that demand will turn higher in most key markets in 2013 as modest restocking replaces destocking this year but that this growth will be relatively muted. It is an expected 8.5% upturn in China that will drive global demand up some 5.6% in 2013, from the subdued 1.9% pace of this year. - With concentrate production capability of mines set to rise more quickly than smelter capacity over the next year, it is likely that the negotiations between mines and smelters for long-term benchmark TC/RCs for 2013 that got underway this month will lead to a rise from 2012 levels of $63.5/t and 6.35c/lb. However, with the exact start date of major new projects such as Oyu Tolgoi remaining unclear and with existing producers such as Collahuasi, Los Bronces and Grasberg failing to meet expectations in 2012, the market remains sceptical as to what extent the increases in mine production forecast for 2013 will materialise. Copper prices surged during September, adding around $1000/t to push copper back through the $8000/t barrier to trade comfortably around the $8200/t level. Much of the increase was the result of central bank easing as we highlighted in our last report. The momentum was further enhanced as traders built up long positions on both COMEX and the LME to push 3-month prices back above the $8300/t level by early October. CFTC data highlights that while net long positions peaked at a high of 11,819 contracts on 9th October, these have since been wound down as the month has progressed. On the LME, renewed buying interest throughout September as indicated by both rising prices and rising open interest has been replaced by long liquidation throughout October with both falling prices and declining open interest. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

Indeed as the stimulus of QE waned through October, macro realities have come back to centre stage. In the days running up to LME week copper had given back over $300/t of the $1000/t September gain. Three month copper prices have subsequently traded lower and fell back below $8000/t by the 23rd October. This decline came on the back of a stronger US dollar and weak economic data out of the Eurozone. Confidence was dented by the slump in German business sentiment which unexpectedly fell to its lowest level in more than 2½ years and registered a sixth straight monthly decline. Although subsequent indicators out of the USA and China have been positive (US economic growth picked up steam to expand at a slightly faster 2% annual rate from July to September, up from the 1.3% rate in the April to June quarter, while the latest HSBC flash China manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), an indicator of the state of factory orders, moved up to 49.1 in October, from 47.9 in September), prices failed to react positively. Copper has continued to remain under pressure amid weak corporate earnings and persistent concerns about global growth with 3-month prices declining to lows of $7670/t during intra day trading. This lack of conviction about the economic outlook is unlik

ely to change until the political uncertainties over the upcoming US presidential elections and the once-in-adecade power transition in Chinese leadership are played out.  At the time of writing, 3-month prices had recovered to levels of around $7770/t supported by buying in the dips.  This was despite recent net inflows of inventories into LME warehouses of 20.725kt over the past couple of days.  The bulk of the increase had been a net 21.3kt delivery into Antwerp which has more than doubled total LME stocks in Europe to 42.825kt, while inventories across Asia and North America have nudged lower.  It is worth noting that total inventories of 488kt across the three exchanges (LME 241kt, Comex 55kt and SHFE 193kt) are still well below the ~700kt estimated in bonded warehouses in China. 

**Waiting on events** These concerns are being mirrored in the physical market with spot interest decidedly absent across the major consuming regions.  In the USA, consumers are looking ahead to the mid-November American Copper Council meeting when they will enter into discussions with producers regarding their 2013 long-term contracts.  In the meantime, both the upcoming elections and now the shadow of Hurricane Sandy are ensuring that consumers are well out of the market and looking to run down any surplus inventories that they may have in their yards.  The lack of spot interest in the market combined with increased availability of scrap has led to a softer tone in US spot premia which are currently been quoted in the 5-6c/lb range compared to the higher levels of 6-7c/lb noted in our publication last month.  This is despite the spectre of extended delivery times for material out of warehouses. 

European markets remain heavily shrouded in a blanket of uncertainty.  Moreover, the latest announcement by Ford that it will cut jobs with the closure of three European plants will dent sentiment and add a further layer of disappointment to the overall economic woes pervading the region.  The automotive market had been the strongest performer in Europe so

far this year and while not immediate, these closures will take their toll on demand prospects in the upcoming years. European spot demand has all but disappeared and as in the USA, scrap remains readily available.  However, with only ~43kt of copper cathode in warehouses across the region, spot premia are being supported and have been quoted in a range of $75-85/t, although there is hardly any liquidity in this market.  European consumers reduced their volumes against long-term contracts for 2012 and left themselves open to the vagaries of the scrap and spot cathode markets even with limited volumes (50kt at the end of December 2011) in LME sheds.  This proved to be the right decision as consumers were, in the main, able to buy cathode on (spot) terms lower than the annual benchmark premia of $90/t. Others were able to su

pplement their requirements with scrap in place of cathode. Persistent uncertainty and the lack of any sign of economic recovery or indeed clarity as to how these debt problems will be resolved in the region would suggest that, once again, European semi fabricators are likely to leave themselves exposed to the risk of higher spot premia in 2013 than carry the cost of financing cathode inventories that could build if there were to be a significant mismatch between demand and order books next year. #### **European premia ($/t)** 160

**One way traffic for cathode flows** China, as the largest consumer of cathode, will be key to the direction of the copper market. End-use demand is lacklustre and although there are some positive signs in the form of an increase in the PMI figures as outlined above, spot interest is very weak with premia currently in the $40-60/t range in October and with levels as low as $30/t being quoted. Copper demand has yet to show any sign of meaningful recovery and in our view this is unlikely to change for some time, given the succession of political power from President Hu Jintao to Vice President Xi Jinping which will be completed later in November. This is despite a marked shift in the underlying structure of the downstream sector where we have noted both expanding refined-intensive rod capacity and the replacement of semis imports by domestically manufactured products. Chinese copper demand has been kept in check not only by slower domestic requirements but also by weaker export growth. September trade data showed a 15% increase month-on-month in net refined copper trade, although the 287kt net inflow was the lowest monthly increase on a year-on-year basis of just 4.9%. However, with significant levels of inventories already sitting in China, the 50% increase in net cathode imports of 2.467Mt in the year to September does offer further bearish news to this market. We believe that the bulk of this latest inflow of metal is a reflection of copper under long-term contract arriving early ahead of the October holiday booked with the expectation of an upturn in consumption, rather than any uptick in spot interest given that the arbitrage has been firmly in negative territory. We are also of the view that some of this material has inevitably ended up in bonded warehouses, raising these stocks to a hefty -700kt (end-October), and in stark contrast to levels of ~240kt at the end of Q3 2011, as the bulk of consumers are reluctant to rebuild inventories at their facilities given the tenuous economic outlook both on the domestic and international front. Given these conditions, it will be interesting to see how the negotiations for long-term contracts play o

ut for 2013 when discussions begin in earnest during the latter half of November. Preliminary feedback is mixed, but on balance suggests that the Chinese will look to reduce their commitments on their 2013 contract volumes and we understand they have asked for terms well below the $110 reportedly offered by Codelco last year. Indeed after PPC’s announcement of a $15/t reduction on premia to $85/t for 2013 early on in October, it would seem likely that the Chilean producers may be under pressure to also offer a similar level of discount on their terms. It would not be surprising if the Chinese reduced their contracted volumes for 2013, given both the high level of inventories in the country but also expanding domestic output and a recent rise in scrap imports. However it is in 2013 that we now reflect a rather more muted surplus. Since our last monthly publication, we have shaved off ~120kt of mine production (before disruptions) as we have reassessed our expectations at several sites. Key changes reflect lower (or perhaps no) output at Frontier (DRC), while we have pushed back output from Kolwezi Tailings (DRC) to 2014, compared to our previous expectations of a 2013 start-up. Revi

sions to output at Grasberg and La Caridad make up the bulk of the changes to our estimates in Asia and Latin America. Overall, these adjustments have tempered the supply side response for 2013, which will reduce our surplus from ~320kt previously, to 219kt and will cap stocks at 54 days of consumption compared to our previous estimates of 56 days. The outlook for 2014 has not Metals Market Service Monthly Update - October 2012 Page 4 of 22 Copper Monthly Update significantly changed and we still forecast a meaningful surplus, although as stock days of consumption are expected to remain below our long-term average of 65, prices should remain well supported over the next couple of years. **ETF challenges** Surprisingly the issue of ETFs have resurfaced. These was last a major issue back in 2010 when both Blackrock and JPMorgan were seeking to launch their own physically backed copper (exchange-traded fund) ETFs. Both of these have been subject to SEC approval and have yet to be launched, unlike the physically backed ETF from UK-based ETF Securities which was launched back in October 2010. In the USA, the SEC delayed its ruling on JPMorgan Chase & Co's plan to launch an ETF physically backed by copper for a second time. A new deadline of December 14th 2012 has been set for the SEC to rule on this ETF. The authorities have argued that they still need more time to consider the issues surrounding the fund which has garnered significant opposition from US copper semis fabricators which include Southwire Co, Encore Wire Corp, Luvata and AmRod, as well as Red Kite, a large hedge fund and physical trader, about its potential impact on metal flows and prices. The SEC is also due to rule on the iShares Copper Trust proposed by BlackRock Inc by Dec. 24, but that decision could yet be extended for another 60 days. This comes at a time when the market is suffering from long delivery times out of LME warehouses. In the meantime, there was talk during LME Week which highlighted that the Exchange is considering separate load-out rates for individual metals to ensure that material is not held up by the long queues associated with other metals. If these ETFs are approved, and fully subscribed, they would account for up to 180kt of copper, and essentially all our estimated surplus for 2013 (JPMorgan's fund would store the equivalent of ~62kt and BlackRock's iShares Copper Trust would use up to ~121kt based on a copper price of $8,000/t). Consumers argue that there is not enough metal available outside the exchange networks for immediate delivery to prevent a squeeze in supply because it is tied up in long-term contracts and the extended load-out rates are further distorting what is essentially a tight market. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

There are known, knowns such as European debt and known unknowns like the future Chinese leadership, while there are most certainly unknown unknowns. The one thing that everyone agreed upon was that there was little to no visibility in order books. Wood Mackenzie forecasts that demand will turn higher in most key markets in 2013 as modest restocking replaces destocking this year but that this growth will be relatively muted. It is an expected 8.5% upturn in China that will drive global demand up some 5.6% in 2013, from the subdued 1.9% pace of this year. ### **Western Europe** **Zero visibility in orderbooks** The key themes emerging from LME Week were broadly centred on the prevailing uncertainty surrounding the demand outlook. Orders at semis producers would normally have increased strongly on a month-on-month basis in September following summer shutdowns but the negative economic backdrop and general gloom surrounding European economies stymied that. Rather, there is a generally cautious tone to placing orders, with consumers and semis producers preferring to keep inventory as low as possible. Semis producers and end users across Europe seem to have no clarity at all on what next year will bring. Another key theme is that customers are asking for increased flexibility in both payment terms and in the size of the order itself. Longer payment terms are understandable in the present climate of constrained working capital and still relatively high copper prices. Requests for flexibility in the order itself seem to centre around firms placing an order a month ahead but asking for the option to trim that order midway through the month. **A (less un)favourable turn for demand** The downbeat economic outlook and failure of demand to turn meaningfully higher resul

ted in a sluggish month for copper consumption in October.  The one positive aspect is that at least year-onyear comparisons are becoming less unfavourable given the weakness of the fourth quarter of last year.  This may result in refined demand actually growing by c.1% in Western Europe overall and by around 4% in Germany.  Consumption in Q4 could even enjoy a modest sequential increase relative to the prior quarter, despite the downbeat tone to economic activity.  Weakness has been felt across most of the end use sectors this year, although the transport sector has been by far the best performer as the strength in production of premium German marques, which are copper intensive, supported consumption.  The driver of automotive production was exports of vehicles to Asian markets but these have now slowed and as a result, copper demand from this sector has also waned.  The construction sector remains weak although it would appear that at least the bottom has been reached.  Elsewhere, the electrical infrastructure markets remain the best hope for a near term upturn if regional governments can commit budgets to support the continued growth of renewable wind energy projects. 

**A difficult balancing act in annual cathode negotiations** The combination of sluggish demand, heightened uncertainty over the economic outlook and a relatively tight regional copper market leaves non integrated semis producers with an interesting question ahead of annual cathode negotiations.  On the one hand, mills will want to keep contracted purchases as low as possible given the lack of clarity in their own order books.  However, this will be set against the scarcity of cathode in the region, with material in LME warehouses standing at around 43kt but much of this behind a mountain of aluminium in Vlissingen.  It is for these reasons that it can be hard to purchase spot cathode in Europe and why premia remain elevated despite the relatively sluggish tone to demand.  We understand that some rod mills have lost business at certain times this year because they did not have the cathode to fulfil orders and they will not want to be faced with this situation again.  However, they will also not wish to finance through additional working capital any more copper than is absolutely necessary.  We believe that semis producers will be more concerned by overbooking material given their current concerns over the outlook, which could result in spot premia spiking at certain points during 2013 if demand is better than expected.  The premia for contracted cathode from Codelco to Western Europe in 2013 has been reported as $85/t, down from $90/t last year. 

**Modest restock to lift 2013 consumption** Our forecasts point to a partial recovery in demand next year with the region as a whole growing by 3.9% following an estimated 7.1% decline in 2012.  Industrial activity is forecast to improve in Europe in general following the contraction in IP in most regional economies this year, althou

gh any upturn is likely to be relatively muted.  The end to sliding demand will at least bring an end to destocking, which on its own will raise consumption, but the improvement in sentiment that economic growth will bring is also expected to feed through to healthier end use sectors. 

### **Sweden** 

**Swede dreams are (not) made of this as high copper prices crimp demand** Swedish demand for copper has been pressured somewhat over the last couple of years and is likely to decline further in 2013.  Towards the start of 2011 when copper prices were hitting new record highs Elektrokoppar announced that they would reduce production of wire rod as a result of financing copper at the $10,000/t level that copper exceeded at the time.  Cash copper prices averaged $9645/t in Q1 2011 compared to $7243/t in the first quarter of 2010, which by our calculations would have added around $24M to Elektrokoppar’s working capital requirements.  Rod exports from Sweden declined in the wake of this production cut, down to 67kt in 2011 from 92kt the prior year.  So far in 2012, exports have recovered some of the ground lost in 2011, increasing by 17% in the first seven months of 2012.  At 48kt between January and July, this is still below the 55kt

that was shipped abroad in the corresponding period of 2010.  However, expectations of a slowdown in overseas shipments in the final quarter of 2012 will lead to a full year decline in wire rod production and refined demand in Sweden. 

**Euro travails pressure orderbooks** Sweden is suffering in part because of its exposure to the rest of Europe given that it exports a significant proportion of its industrial production.  The downturn in the mechanical engineering sector has been particularly severe as firms across Europe have cut back on capital investment, although building and construction is also vying for the title of weakest end use sector.  Winding wire is not performing much better but the one area that is holding up relatively well is high voltage power cables.  Resilience in this segment is largely as a result of investment in wind farms and associated submarine power cable projects.  Other power cable sectors face a renewed threat from substitution to aluminium which is making modest inroads into copper cable demand. 

**Restructuring to trim semis production** The negative tone does not end there as following the acquisition of Luvata’s rolled products division by Aurubis in 2011 it was subsequently announced that production at the Finspang plant in Sweden would end by the middle of 2013.  The announcement at the time stated that some of the equipment would be moved to the production site at Zutphen, Netherlands, while some production volumes would be moved to Buffalo in the US.  This does suggest a reduction in overall capacity.  Our analysis of semis trade flows and apparent consumption suggest that this plant

is still operating for now but clearly this will result in a reduction in refined demand in 2013. **Further decline for 2013** For the year as a whole we anticipate that refined copper demand will decline by c.7% in 2012 following on from a contraction the prior year. For 2013 we forecast that refined consumption will decline further as a result of the closure of semis production capacity at Finspang, despite expectations of an improvement in underlying demand conditions. This will likely stem from the need for further investment in electrical infrastructure across Europe over the coming years. ### **China** **Indicators point to improving economy…** Over the past month an increasing number of factors point to improving underlying demand and economic activity in China. Despite the sluggish (for China) tone to GDP with only a 7.4% expansion in the third quarter, industrial production picked up pace in September and PMI data also appears to have turned a corner. Moreover, there is increasing evidence of stocks of some finished goods being at lower levels. This points towards rising production in future to satisfy improving end use demand. We have not even mentioned the 1 trillion Yuan infrastructure plan or the strong wage growth and tame inflation figures which suggest that consumers will weigh in with higher spending. The problem for copper, however, is that none of this has fed through into increased demand for cathode. #### **Chinese semis production – (kt)** 80 1100

**…but no response from semis producers** The key question is when these factors will lead to an increase in consumption, with time running out in 2012. Many of the points made above do indicate an improvement demand in the near term, in particular the fact that stocks of many finished goods are reportedly at low levels. At the same time, output of white goods and air conditioners both rose on a year-on-year basis in September, with AC production up by 27% month on month, although admittedly it is uncertain how much of this increase was brought forward because of holidays in October. Power cable production also enjoyed a strong rise, up by 35% year on year, with cable makers presumably Metals Market Service Monthly Update - October 2012 Page 7 of 22 Copper Monthly Update lifting production in response to increased orders stemming from state grid investment projects. Clearly, these factors taken together point to increased output of semis in the near term, with a consequent increase in demand for refined metal. **Capacity investment underscores our positive outlook** Aside from the p

erformance of end use sectors, one of the fundamental reasons for our confidence in the short, medium and long term outlook for China is investment in semis capacity.  A number of projects have been announced lately, with Amer’s 250kt/y rod line in Liaoning province reportedly having started construction, while Amer also announced that construction of their 500kt/y line in Guangdong would begin in November.  This is in addition to a number of projects that have already been commissioned.  The impact of this collective semis capacity investment is a diminished requirement for imports of semis, while at the same time raising the prospect of increased exports of both semis and copper containing finished goods.  It is important to note that there will be some losses in capacity in China, with smaller mills losing out to the economies of scale that these large mills will achieve.  Nonetheless, the fundamental point is that capacity increases will drive increase in cathode demand for some time yet. 

### **Malaysia** 

**Domestic firms drive output** The downstream copper industry in Malaysia shares many of the characteristics of the economy in general, with a good deal of production ultimately destined for overseas markets.  The exports to GDP ratio is close to 100%, while well over half of domestic copper semis production is exported and this figure would be even higher if exports of copper consuming goods were considered.  Unlike many of its ASEAN neighbours, investment in semis capacity in Malaysia has been largely driven by domestic companies, although that is not to say overseas companies have not invested at all.  Nearby Asian countries such as Thailand and Vietnam have benefitted from greater inward investment largely as a result of their lower labour costs. 

**Slowdown began in Q2** Copper consumption declined sharply during the financial crisis in 2008 and 2009 but bounced back strongly in 2010, rising some 21% to 203kt.  This stellar pace could not be maintained in 2011, with demand growth slowing to 2%, while consumption this year is set to brake further still to around 1%.  Despite a solid start to the year, consumption eased off from the second quarter onwards as semis production waned in the face of a sluggish export market.  So far this year total exports of copper semis by gross weight are down by around 10%, although refined consumption has held up much better and contracted by only around 3% in the first half.  Moreover, the second quarter compares to a particularly strong Q2 in 2011 and it is for this reason that we expect demand for 2012 as a whole to be up slightly on last year. 

**Brighter outlook following 2012 consolidation** We are more positive on prospects for 2013 and beyond, with a 5% expansion in refined demand forecast as domestic semis production is buoyed by recovering export markets.  This will be in the form of both stronger overseas shipments of copper semis and products which consume copper such as air conditione

rs and component parts for electronics.  Beyond 2013, continued urbanisation and growth in electricity consumption will drive investment in the domestic grid which will further support healthy copper demand growth rates. 

### **US** 

**Economy on hold amid election fever** The general feeling in the US market at present is of no clear direction for demand.  Consumers of cathode continue to place small orders as and when they need material and while some market participants put the current lack of direction down to a wait and see attitude ahead of the Presidential election, others disagree.  The dissenters say that general economic conditions are not that good and for every upbeat economic release there is a downbeat one the next day.  In our discussions, the majority view seems to be that large scale investment decisions are on hold until the outcome of the election is known with some firms also putting hiring decisions on hold. 

**Semis output stutters in September** The stuttering nature of economic activity is neatly reflected in production of copper semis and wire rod in particular.  For much of this year one good month has been followed by a bad one, with September experiencing a downturn after the prior two months had threatened to break the trend.  Wire rod production rose by 6% in July and just under 8% in August but this growth momentum came grinding to a halt in September, with output contracting by 0.7% year on year and by 8% on the prior month.  For the first nine months of the year production is up by a muted 1.4% compared to the January to September period of 2011. 

**Building a head of stream** The one major positive for the US economy would appear to be the continued strength in housing starts, which have been running at double-digit growth rates for some time now.  The Fed’s plan to force mortgage rates lower will surely help to maintain this trend which should also feed through into better household appliance sales.  Given the lag between starting construction of a new house and the installation of building wire and then the further wait until white goods are purchased then it is unlikely that a major upturn will be felt in copper demand until later in 2013. 

**Muted prospects for 2013** For the year as a whole we estimate growth in refined consumption of 1% in 2012 before rising to c.2% next year.  Given our relatively upbeat expectations of the construction market next year it would be easy to assume that this growth rate would be higher but there are a number of reasons for our relatively cautious stance.

It is understood that when favourable silver payability included in these deals is taken into consideration then $60/t & 6c/lb can be considered a representative figure when converting these terms into ‘plain vanilla’ TC/RCs. **2013 mating season starts** The gathering of market participants in London for LME week saw the start of negotiations between mines and smelters for long-term benchmark TC/RCs for 2013. Early signs are that these are likely to lead to a modest rise from the 2012 figures of $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb. 2013 is forecast to see the concentrate production capability of mines rise more quickly than smelter capacity, thereby reversing the trend of recent years. With smelter capacity forecast to rise by around 500kt/a of contained copper and mine production set to rise by 1.12Mt/a (after disruptions) it is estimated that smelter utilisation rates wil

l rise from 80.6% in 2012 to 84.8% in 2013.  Although this trend should put upward pressure on TC/RCs it should also be noted that the forecast smelter utilisation rate is still short of the optimum rate of 88% and that concentrate stock levels are forecast to remain at 28 days which is regarded as the minimum acceptable for efficient operation.  Additionally, with the exact start date of major new projects such as Oyu Tolgoi still in doubt and existing producers such as Collahuasi, Los Bronces and Grasberg failing to meet expectations in 2012, the general feeling during LME week was that the market still lacks confidence that miners will deliver as promised in 2013, placing a dampener on the prospects for any substantial rise in TCRCs.  However, with spot terms on the rise, BHPBilliton continuing to operate outside the benchmark system and with several of the other prominent mining companies having experienced production and delivery issues this year, a lower benchmark in 2013 seems unlikely with many market participants expecting a settlement either side of $70/t & 7c/lb.  . 

**Chinese concentrate imports continue to rise** With reports of low concentrate inventories at some major smelters and spot TCRCs on a rising trend, imports of copper concentrate into China during September were 704kt, marginally higher than the August figure of 695kt.  Imports in September took the year to date total to 5.35Mt, 15% higher than the equivalent period during 2011.

**Chinese provinces support state-owned producers** Reports form China suggest that Yunnan and Jiangxi provinces have introduced initiatives to assist copper producers faced with increasing inventories as a result of reduced demand. Under the scheme the two provinces will increase local reserves by buying metal from state-owned enterprises such as Jiangxi Copper and Yunnan Copper. 

**Additions to Chinese smelter capacity** Tongling NonFerrous Metals Group’s new 400kt/a double flash furnace at Jinchang in Anhui province is now expected to be commissioned before the end of this year.  When the new facility enters production it is understood that the existing 180kt/a Ausmelt furnace will be converted to a secondary production facility.  Meanwhile, Shenzhen Xikuang Investing Company is reported to be planning the construction of a 200kt/a integrated smelter and refinery complex at Ruichang in Jiangxi province.  The RMB3.85Bn ($615M) project is understood to have received permitting from the Jiangxi provincial government, but still needs approval a

t a national level from the Ministry of Environmental Protection. 

**New regulations to affect marine transport of copper concentrates** From 1<sup>st</sup> January 2013, the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) under MARPOL Annex V, will restrict residue discharges of bulk materials such as metal concentrates, matte, scrap and slag.  As the global copper industry assesses the practical implications of these regulations, particularly in light of the short time frame for their implementation, the likely outcome would seem to be that facilities to process hold wash water and other residues will need to be installed at ports handling copper concentrates. 

**New concentrate production from Vale** The first production of copper concentrate was reported from the Lubambe mine in Zambia.  The mine, which was formerly known as Konkola North, is controlled by a 50:50 joint venture between Vale and African Rainbow Minerals.  At full capacity Lubambe is forecast to supply ~50kt/a of copper in concentrate to local smelters.  Meanwhile, shipments of concentrate to European smelters from Vale’s Salobo mine in the north of Brazil are also understood to have commenced.  The Salobo mine is forecast to produce 200kt/a of copper in concentrate at full capacity.  During 2011, Aurubis announced the successful commissioning of a ‘fluorine tower’ at its Hamburg smelter. The facility will treat off-gases generated during the processing of concentrates, such as those from Salobo, that have an elevated fluorine content. 

**Ventanas to halt anode slimes treatment** It is reported that Codelco will halt the production of gold and silver from anode slimes at its Ventanas refinery from Q1 next year.  The slimes that are produced during the copper refining process will instead be sold.  The Ventanas plant produced 109koz of gold and 5,300koz of silver during 2011.  The move is intended to reduce liquid waste discharges from the site.  The smelter and refinery complex, which treats concentrates from Codelco’s nearby Andina mine and from state owned minerals company ENAMI, has been under pressure from environmental groups following a sulphur dioxide leakage in March 2011.

## Production news 

**Collahuasi business improvement plan** Output from the Collahuasi mine in northern Chile continued to disappoint with Xstrata reporting that its 44% share of copper in concentrate production amounted to just 23.7kt during the third quarter of 2012, 44% lower than the equivalent period during 2011.  Low output was attributed to poor head grades, low metallurgical recovery and an extended ball mill outage.  Total copper in concentrate output for 2012 is now forecast to be in the region of 250kt compared to 417kt in 2011.  Shareholders are reported to have initiated a business improvement plan at the mine focussed on increasing equipment availability, raising productivity and increasing head grades with the intention of improving annualised production levels to above 400kt/a from 2013.  It understood that the program of improvement work also entails shutting down one of the SAG mills at the site for repairs to the stator during the early part of 2013. 

**Grasberg milling rate improves, but grade remains low** Operations at Grasberg continued to recover from disruptions earlier in the year, with Freeport McMoRan reporting an average milling rate of 187kt/d during Q3 compared to an average rate of 147kt/d during the first half of the year.  However, production remained hampered by low head grades which averaged only 0.63% Cu during the quarter compared to 0.90% during the equivalent period in 2011. Copper in concentrates production during the quarter was ~95kt taking the year to-date total to 2~35kt.  Under the current mine plan it is forecast that higher grade ore will be accessed during the second half of 2013. 

**Escondida production up year-on-year** Although marginally lower than the previous quarter, production reported by BHPBilliton for the Escondida mine during Q3 was substantially up on the equivalent period during 2011 as the mine continued to produce higher grade ore compared to that seen earlier in the year.  BHPBilliton’s 57.5% share of output amounted to 41.6kt of SxEw cathode and 101.2kt of copper in concentrate during Q3 compared to equivalent figures of 32.9kt and 49.9kt in 2011.  Mill head grade averaged 1.35% Cu during the quarter compared to 0.97% Cu a year earlier when production was also hampered by industrial action.  As the mine continues to access higher grade ore through completion of its ‘Ore Access’ Project and mill throughput improves due to the ‘Laguna Seca Debottlenecking’ project BHPBilliton forecasts that output from Escondida during its 2013 financial year will be 20% higher than in FY2012. 

**Chilean labour deals** Two major Chilean producers successfully concluded negotiations with unions over the renewal of labour contracts.  Anglo American and unions at its Los Bronces mine concluded a four year agreement which included a 4% salary increase plus bonuses and loans worth around $33,000.  Anglo also reported that collective agreements had been s

igned with workers at its El Soldado mine and Chagres smelter.  Meanwhile, at the neighbouring Andina operation Codelco clinched a 40 month agreement with workers which included a 3.2% salary rise plus additional

Rio Tinto holds a 51% stake in Turquoise Hill Resources who in turn retains a 66% stake in the Oyu Tolgoi project.

**Konkola Deep milestone** Vedanta’s long awaited Konkola Deep project reached an important milestone with news that the main underground crusher is to be commissioned this month.  Work on the $1.0Bn project to develop the Konkola Deep orebody began in 2006 and has involved sinking three 1000m ventilation shafts together with the main No.4 haulage shaft which extends to 1500m below ground.  Hoisting of ore from the mid level of the No. 4 shaft commenced in April 2010 when mid-shaft loading was commissioned. Sinking of the shaft to

its bottom most point was completed in July 2011 with waste hoisting commencing after the shaft was fully equipped in October 2012. The waste hoisting process is being fully automated and ore hoisting from the bottom shaft level will commence early in 2012. It is understood that the lower areas of the mine still require significant dewatering and development work and it is forecast that ore output will ramp up to a design rate of 20kt/d yielding around 200kt/a of copper in concentrate incrementally over a six-year period. **Boseto ramp up** Discovery Metals reported that as of the end of September 8kdmt of copper-silver concentrate with an average grade of 38% Cu and 640g/t Ag had been produced at its Boseto mine in Botswana since production began in June. As the mine continues to ramp up to full production, forecast to be 30kt/a of copper in concentrate, Discovery Metals was reported to be the subject of a hostile bid from Cathay Fortune Investment Limited. **CAPEX escalation continues** Despite reports of project cancellations affecting other commodities such as coal and iron ore, high profile copper mining projects still seem to be suffering from capital cost escalation. Freeport McMoRan announced that with 30% of the detailed design of its Cerro Verde expansion project now completed it was revising its estimate of the capital cost required to increase the milling rate at the site from 120kt/d to 360kt/d from $4.0Bn to $4.4Bn. Meanwhile, reports in Chile suggest that the estimated costs of increasing throughput at Codelco’s Andina mine from 90 to 244kt/d have risen 21% from an estimate made earlier this year and now stands at $7.5Bn. The anticipated start date for the expansion project is forecast to be 2020.
